column2: quorum ASSUMPTIONS REGISTER
Every assumption this code makes about the world, and the artifact that would prove it wrong.
WHY THIS FILE EXISTS
This project's only reliable finding is that each NEW KIND of instrument finds defects the previous kinds
cannot, and that the cheapest defects come from two places: feeding it a document written by somebody else,
and taking an assertion the project has made and actually executing it.
Both of those are ad hoc. This register makes them systematic. `docs/claims.tsv` records what the software
is PROVEN to do; this records what it BELIEVES and has not checked.
STATUS values, and they are the point of the file:
FALSIFIED  an artifact disproved it. Fixed, with the artifact kept as a fixture. These are the wins.
TESTED     an artifact exercised it and it held.
UNTESTED   believed, never checked. A defect is more likely here than anywhere else in the project.
STRUCTURAL not falsifiable by artifact -- enforced by construction or by a proof.
An UNTESTED row is not a bug report. It is an admission that the code relies on something nobody has
checked, and a statement of exactly what would settle it.

column2: One row means one cause
column4: a worksheet with several causes bulleted in ONE cell
column5: FALSIFIED, and worse than predicted. A bulleted list inside a quoted cell contains NEWLINES, which broke the CSV reader outright: the record was cut at the embedded newline, every column after it shifted, and a deviation with a real safeguard in the file was reported UNPROTECTED. Wrong output with data silently dropped. RFC 4180 multi-line records now read correctly, and PACKED CAUSES reports the packing without splitting it.

column2: The worksheet arrives as CSV with one header row
column4: a real deliverable: XLSX with merged cells, a banner, multi-row headers, or a PDF table
column5: FALSIFIED -- an Excel export carries a banner (study title, facility, date, then a blank row) ABOVE the header, and taking row 1 as the header refused the file outright while quoting the banner back as though it were column names. The header is now SEARCHED for, up to 20 records in, and the skipped count is reported. A binary .xlsx/.xls/.pdf is detected and told to export as CSV instead of having its bytes quoted into an error. Line numbers now count the banner, because a finding nobody can locate in the file is barely a finding. CLOSED FULLY: the standard worksheet has no Deviation column at all -- a deviation IS a guide word applied to a parameter -- and that layout was refused outright. Parameter and Guide Word are now combined ("High" + "Level"), which is also why they must never be used alone: deviations are deduplicated into observations, and combining on the parameter alone was MEASURED to collapse two "Level" rows into one observation carrying both causes, merging overflow and cavitation into a single symptom needing opposite responses. A Parameter column with no Guide Word is refused with that reason stated.

column2: The worksheet is in English
column4: a HAZOP in German, Spanish, Portuguese or Mandarin
column5: FALSIFIED for German, and the predicted failure had already been mitigated by accident -- the Guard::Unclassified fix for DOC-A16 reports unreadable text instead of waving it through, so a German worksheet was never reported CLEAN. Two real gaps remained: "keine" (none) was read as unclassifiable prose rather than UNPROTECTED, a SEVERITY under-report, and "noch festzulegen" was not a deferral. German PAAG now supported end to end (HAZOP-6). Spanish, Portuguese and Mandarin remain UNTESTED and unsupported, stated in the refusal message.

column2: None-like text in Safeguards means unprotected
column4: a worksheet writing "see note 4", "-", "TBD", "under review", or leaving it blank meaning "not assessed"
column5: TESTED and it holds -- blank, "-", and "Not applicable" report UNPROTECTED while "not assessed" reports a DEFERRAL, which is the right distinction: one says nothing protects this, the other says nobody looked. Blank reading as unprotected is the conservative error.

column2: A latched alarm survives its channel going stale
column4: driving a real casebook through the transition and reading the ACTION, not the mask
column5: TESTED and the answer is NO, by design -- an unbelievable channel asserts `unavailable` and none of its thresholds, so the mask never says quiet when it means blind. Safety is preserved only if the casebook reasons about the `unavailable` observation. tank.cb does and holds stop_transfer; a casebook that does not drops to carry_on. Pinned as BIND-4.

column2: cbc's `nothing reasons about X_unavailable` warning matters
column4: a deliberately blind casebook compiled and run across the stale transition
column5: TESTED -- it matters. The warned casebook goes stop_transfer -> carry_on when the transmitter dies mid-alarm, which is the CAPECO accident. Previously the warning was asserted to be important and never demonstrated.

column2: An action reachable by ONE route needs no independence check
column4: compiling the shipped casebooks and listing single-route actions
column5: FALSIFIED -- the check said "one route cannot be non-independent of itself" and skipped them. It hid pump.cb's SAFE action: `shutdown safe when bearing_wear`, and `bearing_wear needs vib_high bearing_temp_high`. The safe state of the reference casebook is reachable by one route through two sensors, and the check reported the `maintain` action as a win on its first run while saying nothing about this. SOLE ROUTE report added, marked * when it is the safe action. Now finds 3 of 6 shipped casebooks; silent on the two built with redundancy.

column2: A shared safeguard is only worth reporting on a document of at least 3 rows
column4: a 2-row extract where both rows name the same safeguard
column5: FALSIFIED -- reported 0 shared layers at 100% sharing. A single-node extract of a few rows is exactly what a customer sends as a first sample, so the floor hid the finding in the most likely first document. Floor lowered to 2 with the row count printed so the reader can weigh the evidence.

column2: Unreadable safeguard text can be treated as protection
column4: a worksheet whose Safeguards cells say "See note 4" or "TBD pending review"
column5: FALSIFIED -- both were reported as fully protected, identical to a tagged TSH-301 trip. Found via mutation testing: deleting the Instrument classification left the whole suite green because a `Guard::Other` fallback absorbed it. Now DEFERRED and UNCLASSIFIED are reported; only a tagged instrument counts as an IPL candidate.

column2: Each row names a distinct cause
column4: a worksheet where one component failure is written up under several deviations
column5: FALSIFIED -- the hospital-oxygen HAZOP writes "Failure and burning of the solenoid valve" under Over pressure of gas and "Failure and burning of solenoid valve" under Over voltage: same node, same component, one word apart. The importer emitted two unrelated claims, inverting the diagnosis -- one likely fault read as several improbable ones. SHARED CAUSE report added.

column2: Safeguards are ONE column
column4: an industrial HAZOP splitting Preventive from Mitigative safeguards
column5: FALSIFIED, and it produced a FALSE POSITIVE rather than a miss: with Preventive "None" and Mitigative "PSV-203 relief to flare", the deviation was reported UNPROTECTED while a real relief device sat in the next column. A false finding damages credibility worse than a missed one. The second column is now read, and MITIGATIVE ONLY names the case where nothing PREVENTS the deviation and only the consequence is reduced.

column2: A safeguard either exists or does not
column4: a HAZOP recording safeguard INTEGRITY -- SIL rating, proof-test interval, "assumed tested annually"
column5: FALSIFIED silently -- "FAL-105 alarm (never proof tested)" and "PSV-203 (assumed tested annually - no record)" were both counted as full protection layers because the cell contained a tag. A tagged instrument nobody has tested is not a protection layer, it is an assumption with a part number, and it is a hidden failure by definition. UNPROVEN LAYER now reports what the document already admits.

column2: A safeguard phrase belongs to one of four kinds
column4: a worksheet using synonyms outside the keyword lists -- "field check", "surveillance", "rounds", "attended operation"
column5: FALSIFIED conservatively -- "field check", "operator surveillance", "attended operation" and "routine rounds by technician" were all reported as text the tool cannot classify. Reported rather than waved through, so the direction was safe, but calling an obvious human check unclassifiable weakens every finding around it. All four phrasings and eight more now classify as human inspection.

column2: A casebook with no defeaters is not worth shipping
column4: an FTA, which is pure AND/OR with no defeaters at all
column5: TESTED and the prediction was right -- a fault tree transcribed as pure AND/OR over basic events fails validation with "at least one claim can be argued against (3 states)", writes no output, and exits 1. An FTA records what can fail, never why a conclusion might not follow, so it cannot become a casebook without an engineer adding defeaters.

column2: Preference-dependent attacks from strictly-less-severe claims can be dropped
column4: a casebook where dropping one changes an outcome
column5: TESTED and it demonstrably matters -- two fixtures differing only in the rebutting claim's severity: at severity 2 against a severity-9 claim the attack is cancelled and the safe action holds in 2 of 4 states; at equal severity it stands and the safe action holds in 1 of 4. Dropping the weaker attack makes the device act MORE often, which is the conservative direction. Pinned as SEV-1.

column2: The hand-transcribed Cortex-M33 instruction costs are right
column4: real silicon sweeping all 16,384 states
column5: TESTED on 2026-09-28/29 on both cores, and it holds. On the Cortex-M33 the costs were transcribed for (Raspberry Pi Pico 2, 150 MHz), the slowest solve in three runs is 3,719 cycles against the 2,571-instruction bound = 1.45 cycles per instruction; on a Cortex-M4 (Uno R4, 48 MHz) 3,608 cycles = 1.40. Both under the 2 CPI the README conversion assumes. Both devices took exactly the 140 steps cbc predicted, inside the proven 248, and on the Pico 2 a 16,384-state sweep run on the silicon picked the same worst state as kWorstCaseMask. The bound transfers between the cores: tools/wcet-disassemble.sh gives an identical instruction count and opcode mix for cortex-m33 and cortex-m4. The framing originally recorded here was WRONG: "measured max must come under 2,571" compared cycles to instructions, which are different units.

column2: The published footprint cannot usefully be reduced
column4: measuring the arrays against the index range they actually hold
column5: FALSIFIED as a size claim -- all seven index arrays are std::int32_t for values that never exceed 45, because the compiler refuses past 30 observations. int16_t indices save 834 B on pump and 800 B on tank: 48% of RAM. NOT implemented: it touches MISRA-relevant engine code for space nobody has asked for. Measured floor for a complete minimal safety function is 1,030 B flash / 348 B RAM; the engine's own code is 444 B.

column2: A LOPA worksheet lays out its layers as marked columns
column4: a real published LOPA table
column5: TESTED against the biocontainment study (Sci Rep 15:4428, CC BY). Its Table 4 heads the PFD columns A/B/C/D with a SEPARATE legend table mapping each letter to a description, which a CSV cannot hold. The importer therefore requires the layer kind to be MARKED in the header (IPL/CM) and refuses to guess which columns hold PFDs, because guessing wrong in either direction changes the arithmetic silently -- a missed layer makes the scenario look worse than the document says, and a non-PFD column read as a PFD makes it look better.

column2: A layer that names the system which failed is not independent of it
column4: applying the check to a real document and counting the false positives
column5: FALSIFIED by measurement, in the false-positive direction. The first version matched any shared system family and reported "Blockage in the drainage header" against "Drainage level switches available in every drain" -- twice, on a published paper. A level switch inside a drain is not defeated by that drain blocking; detecting it is what the switch is for. The check now considers only SUPPORT systems a layer needs in order to FUNCTION (control system, power, instrument air, ventilation) plus the human factor, which cut four findings to the two that are defensible.

column2: An FMEA is the weakest document for every purpose
column4: reading what an FMEA actually contains that a HAZOP does not
column5: FALSIFIED as a general claim, and it had been the project's own claim. An FMEA is the weakest for BUILDING A CASEBOOK -- it has no Safeguards column, so not one of the protection-layer questions can be asked of it. But it states S, O, D and an RPN, so like a LOPA it asserts a conclusion and shows its working, which makes it auditable by arithmetic rather than by reading English. The ranking conflated two different purposes. STILL OPEN: unlike the HAZOP and LOPA detectors, these have never run against a real third-party FMEA, because both real FMEAs found are CC BY-NC-ND and forbid derivative works.

column2: A stub Arduino.h proves the staged sketch is portable
column4: compiling the staged sketch with a real vendor BSP
column5: FALSIFIED by the first real toolchain the code ever met. Gate 15 compiles the staged sketch for cortex-m4 against a STUB Arduino.h and passed throughout, while the actual Arduino core rejected the code twice over: an enumerator named SysTick, which CMSIS defines as `#define SysTick ((SysTick_Type *) SysTick_BASE)`, and a function named bit(), which the Arduino core defines as `#define bit(b) (1UL << (b))`. In both cases the preprocessor rewrote quorum's own declarations and GCC reported the error inside the vendor header, far from the cause. A stub is only hostile in the ways you remember to make it hostile. Now Source::Systick and obs_bit(). The gate still has value -- it proves self-containment -- and it cannot substitute for a real BSP.

column2: The Arduino build puts the sketch folder on the include path
column4: reading the compiler command line arduino-cli generates
column5: FALSIFIED. It never does. Quoted includes therefore resolve only relative to the including FILE, so the .ino could find quorum/arbiter/verdict.hpp while that header's own "quorum/solver/framework.hpp" could not -- it was looked for at quorum/arbiter/quorum/solver/. Two wrong fixes were tried first (a src/ subfolder in the sketch, then an explicit -I) before reading the generated command line settled it. The headers now stage as a LIBRARY, whose src/ IS on the include path, which is the only arrangement that works in the IDE as well as the CLI.

column2: A measured maximum on the target part is a stable number
column4: repeating the same measurement on the same RP2350 across separate flashes
column5: FALSIFIED on the Pico 2. Three runs of identical firmware on the same board gave solve maxima of 3,466, 3,719 and 3,681 cycles and warm full-cycle maxima of 12,827, 13,988 and 15,223, while the solve MINIMUM was 2,809 or 2,810 every time. The algorithm is deterministic; the RP2350 fetches code from QSPI flash through a cache, and the maximum depends on cache state. The same measurement on the cacheless RA4M1 returned min = mean = max exactly on two flashes. Consequence: on a cached part, "measured WCET" from a single run is not reproducible, which is the general argument for a static bound made concrete. The README quotes the worst of three runs and says so; the instruction bound is the guaranteed figure.

column2: Vanilla AA-CBR can be run on real data as published
column4: learn/eval/eval_learn.cpp voting, Coherence::KeepAll
column5: FALSIFIED on the first real dataset tried. AA-CBR assumes a coherent casebase -- no two cases with the same features and different outcomes -- and real data is not coherent. The method counts ARGUMENTS, not evidence: on the voting data restricted to one vote, 245 democrats and 2 republicans shared a pattern, duplicates collapsed to one argument each, the republican one attacked the default with nothing more specific to defend it, and all 245 were classified republican. Accuracy 39.77% at k = 2, below the 61.38% of always guessing the majority. Repaired by Coherence::MajorityPerPattern (one case per pattern, majority outcome, a tie contributes nothing), which scores 95.63% at the same k. The repair is this implementation's choice and is named as such.

column2: AA-CBR over raw features generalises like a case-based method
column4: learn/eval/eval_learn.cpp voting, section 1
column5: FALSIFIED. A past case speaks about a query only if the query has EVERY one of the case's features. On the voting data a case carries about 15 of 32 features, and 229 of 435 queries had two or fewer relevant past cases. With all 32 features AA-CBR scored 81.38% against 93.10% for plain 1-nearest-neighbour. Feature selection is therefore not optional for this method; it is also what fits a learned casebook inside the 30-observation limit a device imposes.

column2: A learned argumentation casebook is competitive on accuracy with a plain case-based learner
column4: learn/eval/eval_learn.cpp on two UCI datasets, identical protocol
column5: FALSIFIED. Under the same folds, seed and nested selection, 1-NN matched or beat AA-CBR on both datasets tried: 95.40 against 95.63 on voting (a tie, because every method collapses onto one vote), and 98.64 against 84.03 on tic-tac-toe, where the methods diverge. The reason is structural and stated in the code: a past case speaks about a query only if the query holds every one of its features, so AA-CBR generalises only as far as the feature encoding makes cases nest. One-hot encodings (cell is x / o / blank) make them never nest. Whatever argumentation offers a learned casebook, on this evidence it is not accuracy -- the case for it has to rest on what 1-NN does not give: a derivation that can be audited, an exhaustive check of every input state, and a proven step bound. Those are claims to test, not to assume.

column2: Data can safely be allowed to refine a reviewed rule with any more specific exception
column4: learn/eval/eval_monks.cpp, learn/data/monks/monks-3.train
column5: FALSIFIED by the pre-registered MONK-3 replication. Its training set has 6 deliberately wrong labels; with the complete, correct casebook the hybrid turned single records into exceptions and made 12 mistakes the casebook alone did not (100.00 to 97.32). Repaired by the exception guard: a learned case may attack a reviewed rule only with 2 or more supporting records. On 200 fresh problems that took "within 1 point of the complete casebook" from 167/200 to 196/200, at no measurable cost in wins.

column2: Adding learning to an incomplete casebook reliably clears a pre-registered bar
column4: learn/PREREGISTRATION.md, learn/eval/eval_synth.cpp
column5: FALSIFIED as stated. Four pre-registered tests, four verdicts of NOT SHOWN. The AVERAGE gain was large every time (+8.37, +19.87, +14.58, +18.41 points), but the win rate missed its bar in three of the four, because learning gains nothing when the missing knowledge is redundant or inexpressible in the available observations, and occasionally loses. What survives is narrower: large average gains, almost never worse (195/200 fresh problems), and no damage to a correct casebook once the exception guard is in place.

column2: A learned casebook is something an argumentation engine is needed for
column4: learn/test/test_learned_casebook.cpp, build/learn/learned (generated)
column5: TESTED -- and only sometimes true. Of six learned MONK casebooks, cbc accepted two, which contain learned exceptions, and refused four as pure rule lists ("nothing is defeasible ... a decision tree"), the same verdict it gives a raw FMEA import. Argumentation earns its place in a learned casebook only when the data contains exceptions to rules; when it does not, the honest output is a rule list.
